title: Predicting Suppressors of Cell-Death Pathways from Transcriptomic Data
author: Vinik, Maimon, et al.

steps.title: Seed 96-well plates for dose‑response
steps.instruction: One day before treatment, seed each cell line into 96‑well plates at a cell number that will give ≤50 % confluency on the day of drug addition; determine the exact seeding density for each line based on its growth rate and cell size and keep conditions identical across all wells.

steps.title: Add drug dilutions and controls
steps.instruction: After 24 h, replace medium with fresh medium containing a series of increasing drug concentrations that have been pre‑determined to give ~100 % viability at the lowest dose and <25 % viability at the highest dose; include triplicate wells for each concentration, maintain identical DMSO (or other solvent) volume in every well, keep DMSO ≤0.1 % (v/v), and add untreated control wells containing the same solvent volume but no drug.

steps.title: Incubate and perform viability assay
steps.instruction: Incubate plates at 37 °C in a humidified 5 % CO₂ incubator; 72 h after drug addition, assess cell viability with an MTT assay (or equivalent).

steps.title: Calculate % viability per concentration
steps.instruction: For each drug concentration, compute the average viability of the triplicate wells and express it as a percentage of the average viability of the untreated control wells.

steps.title: Determine IC50 from dose‑response data
steps.instruction: Using the dose‑response curves generated above (and the provided code in step 1b of the original manuscript), calculate the IC₅₀ value for each drug in each cell line.

steps.title: Seed 6‑well plates for transcriptomics
steps.instruction: Seed the same cell lines into 6‑well plates at a density that will reach ≤50 % confluency on the day of treatment; adjust the cell number for each line accordingly.

steps.title: Treat cells at IC50 and collect controls
steps.instruction: Twenty‑four hours after seeding, replace medium with medium containing each drug at its previously determined IC₅₀ concentration; include vehicle‑control wells that receive the same volume of solvent (e.g., DMSO) as the treated wells; perform at least three biological replicates for each condition.

steps.title: Extract RNA and perform RNA‑seq
steps.instruction: Four to twenty‑four hours after drug addition, harvest cells and extract total RNA using a standard method such as Trizol; subsequently generate RNA‑seq libraries and sequence them; the final output should be a count matrix with genes as rows and treatment conditions as columns.

steps.title: Install R and required packages
steps.instruction: Download and install R 4.4.0 (https://cran.r‑project.org/) and RStudio (https://www.rstudio.com/); in RStudio, run the following commands to install and load the needed packages: install.packages(c("tidyverse","drc","cmapR","umap","rentrez","ggrepel")); if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager"); BiocManager::install(c("PharmacoGx","limma","cogena","fgsea")); library(tidyverse); library(drc); library(PharmacoGx); library(cmapR); library(umap); library(rentrez); library(limma); library(cogena); library(fgsea); library(ggrepel).

steps.title: Aggregate predictor data into a table
steps.instruction: Combine the correlation predictors (Step 4 of the original protocol) and the transcriptomic similarity predictors (Step 9) into a single data frame where each row corresponds to a gene and columns contain: AUC correlation to expression for each inducer, AUC correlation to gene‑effect (depscore) for each inducer, and transcriptomic similarity scores for each cell‑line/inducer combination (as illustrated in Table 3).

steps.title: Compute combined scores and rank genes (best predictors)
steps.instruction: Using the aggregated data frame, calculate for each gene: (a) mean_r_expression = row mean of all “AUC cor to expression” columns; (b) mean_r_depscore = row mean of all “AUC cor to depscore” columns; (c) biggest_r = max(mean_r_expression, mean_r_depscore); (d) mean_CMAP_scores = row mean of all transcriptomic similarity columns; (e) rank_corr_expression = rank of mean_r_expression (min‑rank); (f) rank_corr_depscore = rank of mean_r_depscore; (g) rank_corr = max(rank_corr_expression, rank_corr_depscore); (h) rank_CMAP_score = rank of mean_CMAP_scores; (i) mean_rank = (rank_corr + rank_CMAP_score)/2; (j) rank_total = min‑rank of mean_rank. Implement these steps with the dplyr pipeline shown in the original code. Finally, list the genes with the highest rank_total as top candidates.

steps.title: Visualize top‑ranked genes
steps.instruction: Create a scatter plot of the intermediate scores (rank_corr on the y‑axis, rank_CMAP_score on the x‑axis) and highlight the genes with the highest rank_total (top‑left corner of the plot) as done in Figure 2A of the source article.

steps.title: Perform UMAP dimension reduction on predictors
steps.instruction: Using the same combined predictor data frame, run UMAP to project all genes into a 2‑D space: set seed 42; scale all numeric columns; apply umap() (or the equivalent code snippet provided); plot the resulting map with gene labels as needed (see the code block in the original protocol).

steps.title: Compute distances to key pathway gene and rank (nearest neighbors)
steps.instruction: Select one or more key genes of the pathway (e.g., GCH1 for ferroptosis); for each gene, compute Euclidean distance to the key gene using distance = sqrt((U1‑Ukey)² + (U2‑Vkey)²); create a table of gene and distance, sort ascending, and extract the top 75 closest genes as the nearest‑neighbor ranking.

steps.title: Select top candidate genes for validation
steps.instruction: From the ranked list obtained in step 13 (best predictors) or step 14 (nearest neighbors), take the top 75 genes as the primary candidate set for experimental follow‑up.

steps.title: Conduct automated PubMed search for novelty
steps.instruction: Using the rentrez package, query PubMed for each of the 75 genes combined with each of the pathway‑specific terms: "Ferroptosis", "Lipid peroxidation", "Iron", "Glutathione", "GPX4", "SLC7A11". Set your personal NCBI API key via set_entrez_key("PUBMED_KEY"). For each gene‑term pair, record the hit count; store the results in a tibble and save as "Pubmed search for ranked list.RData". This step filters out genes already heavily associated with the pathway.

steps.title: Optionally filter for druggability and toxicity
steps.instruction: Cross‑reference the candidate gene list with DepMap (https://depmap.org/portal/) to obtain druggability information from each gene’s “overview” page and to flag genes labeled as “common essential” (high toxicity). Retain only genes that are druggable and not common essentials, if desired.

steps.title: Experimentally validate selected genes
steps.instruction: Target each shortlisted gene in the relevant cancer cell lines using shRNA, siRNA, or CRISPR‑sgRNA; after knock‑down/knock‑out, assess the hallmarks of the death pathway under study (e.g., ferroptosis markers) as described in the authors’ previous publication (see Figure 5 of Vinik et al.).

steps.title: Perform statistical GSEA validation of rankings
steps.instruction: Download pan‑cancer gene‑expression data (CCLE) and drug‑sensitivity data (CTRP) from DepMap; for each gene, compute the correlation between its expression and the AUCs of the ferroptosis‑inducing drugs (e.g., erastin, ML210, ML162); create a vector of correlation scores for all genes; run fgsea() with the top‑ranking gene set (the 75 candidates) against this ranked list (maxSize = 1000, scoreType = "std"); visualize enrichment with plotEnrichment(); optionally generate a scatter/violin plot of correlation distributions as in the original code.

description: In this protocol, we merge two drug discovery approaches to reliably predict candidate genes that suppress cancer cell death pathways. In the first approach, we use a set of cell death inducers to define vulnerabilities across multiple cancer cell lines, and then correlate the vulnerabilities to public datasets of gene expression and gene essentiality in cancer cell lines. High correlations highlight genes whose targeting may increase vulnerability to the death pathway. In the second approach, we profile the transcriptomic response of the death inducers by RNA sequencing in several breast cancer cell lines. We then compare these transcriptomic responses to the transcriptomic response signatures induced by gene silencing using public datasets of thousands of transcriptomic signatures (Connectivity Map; CMAP, Broad Inst.). We quantify the transcriptomic similarity and rank the genes according to their similarity scores. Subsequently, we merge the two approaches and generate a single metric that measures the potential of each gene to be a death repressor and consequently a possible target for cancer therapy. Two methods have been used for merging: (i) aggregating the scores of the two approaches into a single metric, and (ii) using a dimension reduction method to project all the scores on a 2D plane and measure the distances between the genes and a central key gene of the pathway. Throughout this protocol, we employed several computational validation approaches, and subsequently experimentally validate the selected genes. This protocol could be powerful for any drug that induce cell death. The inputs are (i) the vulnerability of the cell lines to the drug which can be measured by dose response curves, and (ii) the transcriptomic response profile of the drug based on RNA-seq data.
